notes:
Task and constraints: Arrange cards into groups of consecutive values of size groupSize.
Idea: Count values and repeatedly start a group from the smallest remaining value using a min-heap.
Technique and why it applies: Every group must begin at the smallest unused value; decrement each consecutive value and remove a value from the heap when its count reaches zero.
Invariant: freq stores remaining multiplicities and the heap tracks values still represented.
Edge cases: collections and heapq are referenced without imports in this snippet. A missing value or premature count exhaustion returns false; groupSize is assumed positive.
Complexity: Heap operations and frequency processing take O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether the hand can be split into consecutive groups of W cards.
Idea: Count frequencies, heapify card values, and repeatedly build groups starting from the smallest remaining card.
Technique and why it applies: Each group consumes W consecutive values; negative frequency means a required card was unavailable.
Invariant: counts records remaining copies and the heap supplies low card values first.
Edge cases: The heap contains all hand entries, including duplicates; zero-count roots are removed before each group. W must be positive and divide hand length.
Complexity: Heap operations take O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the shortest walk that visits every node in a connected graph.
Idea: Compute all-pairs shortest distances, then memoize a subset-DP recurrence for visiting remaining nodes.
Technique and why it applies: The recurrence chooses the next required node and adds its shortest-path distance; trying every starting node gives the minimum walk.
Invariant: fn(node,mask) is intended to return the minimum distance needed to visit the nodes in mask.
Edge cases: inf and cache are used without imports. The recurrence treats shortest paths between nodes as independent legs, and its state transition needs careful validation for revisits.
Complexity: Floyd-Warshall costs O(n³); subset DP is exponential, about O(n²2^n) time and O(n2^n) memo space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of edges in a walk visiting every graph node.
Idea: Run multi-source BFS from every node, storing states as visited-node bitmasks and current endpoints.
Technique and why it applies: Each edge adds one node to the mask and costs one step; BFS explores states by path length.
Invariant: dp[mask][node] stores the shortest distance discovered for that mask and endpoint.
Edge cases: The graph is assumed connected enough to visit all nodes; unreachable full-mask states would remain infinity.
Complexity: There are O(n2^n) states and O(m2^n) transitions, with O(n2^n) time and space.

Task and constraints: Apply cumulative letter shifts where shifts[i] affects the prefix ending at i.
Idea: Accumulate shifts from right to left modulo 26, then shift each character by its total.
Technique and why it applies: A suffix sum gives the total shift affecting each position; modular arithmetic wraps letters within lowercase alphabet.
Invariant: nums[i] stores the cumulative shift for position i.
Edge cases: The code uses a while loop to subtract 26 until the character fits; valid lowercase inputs and nonnegative shifts are assumed.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and auxiliary space O(n) for the shift array and output.

Task and constraints: Apply cumulative shifts to every prefix of a lowercase string.
Idea: Initialize the total with all shifts, emit the shifted first character, then subtract each shift as the scan advances.
Technique and why it applies: At index i, times equals the sum of shifts from i onward, which is exactly the total affecting that character.
Invariant: times stores the remaining suffix sum modulo 26.
Edge cases: Characters are assumed lowercase English letters and shifts align one-to-one with the string.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time with O(n) output storage.

Task and constraints: Choose an empty seat maximizing distance to the nearest occupied seat.
Idea: Collect occupied positions, compare the leading and trailing empty runs, and evaluate gaps between occupied seats.
Technique and why it applies: An interior gap's best seat is midway between occupied endpoints, while an end gap can use its full length.
Invariant: seat_nums stores occupied indices and dists stores each interior gap's best distance.
Edge cases: The code assumes at least one occupied seat; otherwise min and max fail. A nonempty valid seating arrangement is expected.
Complexity: Scanning and collecting positions takes O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the empty seat farthest from any occupied seat.
Idea: Scan occupied seats, using the first seat's index for the leading gap and half-gap distances thereafter.
Technique and why it applies: The distance in an interior interval is floor((i-prev)/2); after the scan, the trailing empty run is checked.
Invariant: prev is the last occupied seat and result is the best distance found.
Edge cases: The implementation initializes result to one and assumes at least one occupied seat; standard constraints guarantee an occupied seat.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Compute the union area of axis-aligned rectangles modulo 10^9+7.
Idea: Sweep horizontal events and use a segment tree over compressed x-coordinates to track covered width.
Technique and why it applies: Between consecutive y events, area increases by vertical distance times current covered x-width; events then update active intervals.
Invariant: cur_x_sum is the covered width at the current sweep height, maintained by the segment tree.
Edge cases: defaultdict is used without an import. The segment-tree recursion assumes valid compressed coordinate indices and nonempty rectangles.
Complexity: Sorting events and updates take O(R log R) time with O(R) compressed-coordinate storage.

Task and constraints: Compute the union area of rectangles using a sweep line and dynamic segment tree.
Idea: Sort opening and closing events by y, maintaining covered x-length in a segment tree.
Technique and why it applies: Before each event, add current covered width times the height difference; then update the x interval for the event.
Invariant: cur_x_sum stores the active union width, and tree nodes store covered length and overlap count.
Edge cases: The code accesses events[0], so an empty rectangle list fails. Coordinates are compressed, and intervals are represented half-open in the tree.
Complexity: Events and tree updates take O(R log R) typical time and O(R) space.

Task and constraints: For each person, find the quietest person among everyone known to be richer or equally rich.
Idea: Topologically process the richer-than directed graph and propagate the quietest known candidate to poorer neighbors.
Technique and why it applies: When a node is processed, its best candidate is compared with each poorer neighbor's candidate; indegrees determine when all richer predecessors have been processed.
Invariant: arr[node] stores the quietest person among the processed richer ancestry including node.
Edge cases: collections is used without import. The richer relation must be acyclic, as guaranteed by the problem.
Complexity: Topological traversal takes O(V+E) time and O(V+E) space.

Task and constraints: Find the peak index in a mountain array.
Idea: Binary-search by comparing each midpoint with its next element.
Technique and why it applies: If the sequence is still rising, move right; otherwise move left to locate the turning point.
Invariant: beg is advanced across rising positions and end retreats on descending positions.
Edge cases: When mid reaches the last index, arr[mid+1] would be out of bounds; the search condition can allow this, so the implementation has a boundary bug.
Complexity: Intended binary search is O(log n) time and O(1) space, but boundary access can fail.

Task and constraints: Find the peak index in a mountain array using binary search.
Idea: Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid+1] and keep the side containing the rise-to-fall transition.
Technique and why it applies: A rising pair means the peak is to the right; a falling pair means the peak is at or to the left.
Invariant: left and right bound the possible peak position.
Edge cases: The loop can set mid to the last index and access arr[mid+1], so this implementation may raise an index error unless bounds are tightened.
Complexity: Intended time is O(log n) with O(1) extra space, subject to the boundary issue.

Task and constraints: Count fleets of cars reaching target without passing one another.
Idea: Sort cars by position from closest to target backward and compare their arrival times.
Technique and why it applies: A car forms a new fleet only if it arrives later than the fleet ahead; faster cars behind merge into that fleet.
Invariant: arrival_bound is the slowest arrival time of the fleet ahead, and fleet counts distinct arrivals.
Edge cases: The condition not arrival_bound also treats zero time as unset, though positions are normally strictly below target. Sorting preserves position-speed pairs.
Complexity: Sorting takes O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps needed to transform s1 into s2 when they are anagrams.
Idea: Recursively fix the first mismatched position by swapping in a character matching the target there.
Technique and why it applies: Only later positions containing the needed target character are considered; memoization stores costs for each index and current string.
Invariant: dp[i][curr] stores the minimum remaining swaps for the current string from index i onward.
Edge cases: sys is referenced without import. The method assumes anagrams; when no matching later character is found, a large sentinel can be returned.
Complexity: The state space can be exponential in string length, with memo storage depending on encountered strings.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum swaps to transform A into B when the strings are anagrams.
Idea: Use BFS over strings, generating neighbors by swapping the first mismatched character with a later matching target character.
Technique and why it applies: Every swap costs one, and BFS layers guarantee the first arrival at B uses the fewest swaps.
Invariant: lookup prevents duplicate strings and result tracks the current BFS depth.
Edge cases: The neighbor helper assumes a mismatch exists; if a non-target state has no suitable later character, no neighbors are produced.
Complexity: The search can be exponential in n! states, using corresponding time and memory.

Task and constraints: Compute the score of a balanced parentheses string.
Idea: Track nesting depth and add a power of two whenever a closing parenthesis immediately follows an opening one.
Technique and why it applies: A primitive pair nested at depth d contributes 2^(d-1), matching the recursive scoring rule.
Invariant: level is the current nesting depth and result accumulates scores of primitive pairs.
Edge cases: The input is assumed balanced; malformed strings can cause negative or inconsistent depths.
Complexity: The scan takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the score of a balanced parentheses string using a stack.
Idea: Push a zero score for each opening parenthesis; on closing, combine the inner score with the enclosing score.
Technique and why it applies: A pair scores one when its interior is empty, otherwise twice its interior score.
Invariant: Each stack entry stores the accumulated score for one nesting level.
Edge cases: The input is assumed balanced; each close expects a matching opening level on the stack.
Complexity: The stack is O(n) space and the scan is O(n) time.

Task and constraints: Compute the score of balanced parentheses from nesting depth.
Idea: Increase depth on open parentheses, decrease on close, and add 2^depth when a primitive pair closes.
Technique and why it applies: The pair () at current nesting contributes the power corresponding to its surrounding depth.
Invariant: depth tracks active nesting and result accumulates primitive-pair contributions.
Edge cases: The input must be balanced; indexing S[i-1] is safe for a valid string that closes after an opening parenthesis.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum total wage to hire exactly k workers under equal pay-to-quality ratio.
Idea: Sort workers by wage-to-quality ratio and maintain the k smallest qualities in a max-heap.
Technique and why it applies: For a chosen ratio, every selected worker is paid ratio times quality; the k smallest qualities minimize the total under that ratio.
Invariant: kSmallest stores selected quality sum and pq holds negative qualities to simulate a max-heap.
Edge cases: heapq and heappop/heappush are not imported in the snippet. The first k workers initialize the candidate cost.
Complexity: Sorting plus heap updates take O(n log n) time and O(n) space.
